questions.prompt: A 384x640 image is processed with 16x16 patches and no CLS token. How many tokens?
Same image, one head. How many entries does the attention matrix have?
Patch size is halved from 16 to 8 on the same image. By what factor does attention cost per head grow?
Scores for token 3 are (0, 0, 0.7071) over three tokens. What weight does it give itself (3 decimals)?
What is the main reason for dividing QK^T by sqrt(d)?
options: It makes the attention matrix symmetric, so queries and keys can share weights.
It normalises each row of the matrix to unit Euclidean length.
The dot product variance grows with d; scaling keeps the softmax out of saturation.
It reduces the number of tokens that are attended to in each layer.
questions.explanation: Without scaling large scores give a near one-hot softmax with tiny gradients.

questions.prompt: A student shuffles the patches of a test image and the ViT (with learned position codes) gives a different prediction. A colleague says this is a bug. Is it?
options: Yes: the CLS token should not depend on the order of the input patches
No: position codes tie each patch to its slot, so the shuffle changes the input
Yes: attention is permutation-invariant, so shuffled patches must give the same output.
No: shuffling the patches can never change a prediction made by a transformer
questions.explanation: With codes added per slot the model is not equivariant; moved patches look like a different image.

questions.prompt: Which statement about inductive bias is correct?
options: Inductive biases are irrelevant once a model has been pretrained on large data.
A CNN builds in locality and translation equivariance; a ViT assumes little and needs more data.
Both architectures have identical inductive biases and need equal amounts of data.
A ViT assumes locality and translation equivariance more strongly than a CNN, so it needs less data.
questions.explanation: This is why ViTs rely on large data or augmentation.
